'''Don Leslie Lind'''<ref name="nasa198701"/> (May 18, 1930 – August 30, 2022) was an American scientist, [[United States Navy|naval officer]], [[United States naval aviator|aviator]], and [[NASA]] [[astronaut]]. He graduated from the [[University of Utah]] with an undergraduate degree in physics in 1953. Following his military service obligation, he earned a PhD in [[high-energy nuclear physics]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1964.

Lind was a [[United States Naval Aviator|Naval Aviator]] and attained the rank of commander in the [[United States Naval Reserve]]. After completing his doctorate, Lind worked at NASA's Goddard Research Center from 1964 to 1966. Selected with [[Astronaut Group 5]] in 1966, he helped to develop the Apollo 11 EVA activities, and served as CAPCOM for the [[Apollo 11]] and [[Apollo 12]] missions. Lind was then assigned as backup pilot for [[Skylab 3]] and [[Skylab 4]] and would have flown on [[Skylab Rescue]].

Lind was the payload commander on his only flight, [[STS-51-B]], launched April 29, 1985. He designed an experiment to capture the Earth's aurora. The payload experiments consisted primarily of microgravity research and atmospheric measurement. The [[Space Shuttle Challenger|Orbiter ''Challenger'']] completed 110 orbits before landing at [[Edwards Air Force Base]], California.

== Biography ==

=== Early life and education ===
Lind was born May 18, 1930, and raised in [[Midvale, Utah]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=writer |first=By Charles McCollum staff |date=2022-09-02 |title=Cache Valley resident and former astronaut Don Lind dies at 92 |url=https://www.hjnews.com/news/local/cache-valley-resident-and-former-astronaut-don-lind-dies-at-92/article_ffd33230-2aec-11ed-8411-4f15162502a3.html |access-date=2025-07-29 |website=The Herald Journal |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-09-02 |title=Don Lind, Latter-day Saint astronaut, scientist, pilot, dies at age 92 |url=https://www.thechurchnews.com/members/2022/9/2/23332941/don-lind-latter-day-saint-astronaut-scientist-dies-at-age-92/ |access-date=2025-07-29 |website=Church News |language=en}}</ref> with his two sisters, Charlene and Kathleen. He attended Midvale Elementary School and graduated from [[Jordan High School (Sandy, Utah)|Jordan High School]] in 1948. He was an [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]] with the [[Boy Scouts of America]], its highest rank.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scouting.org/FILESTORE/pdf/02-558.pdf|title=Astronauts and the BSA|publisher=Boy Scouts of America|access-date=June 6, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110622104220/http://www.scouting.org/FILESTORE/pdf/02-558.pdf|archive-date=June 22, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref> He received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree with high honors in [[physics]] from the [[University of Utah]] in 1953.<ref name="nasa198701">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/lind_don_0.pdf |title=Astronaut Bio: Don Lind |publisher=NASA |date=January 1987 |access-date=April 4, 2021 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210518121259/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/lind_don_0.pdf |archive-date=May 18, 2021 }}</ref>

As a [[United States Naval Aviator|Naval Aviator]], Lind volunteered to take high-altitude [[photo emulsion]]s of [[cosmic rays]] for the [[University of California, Berkeley]] during flights. This helped him enroll at Berkeley,<ref name="utahalum">{{Cite web |title=Honor Roll |url=http://www.alumni.utah.edu/u-news/august09/?display=honor_roll.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629164308/http://www.alumni.utah.edu/u-news/august09/?display=honor_roll.html |archive-date=2011-06-29 |website=U-News & Views |publisher=University of Utah Alumni Association}}</ref><ref name="moulton20090720">{{Cite web |last=Moulton |first=Kristen |date=July 20, 2009 |title=Utah astronaut recalls his role in moon walk |url=http://www.sltrib.com/news/ci_12868837 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090821230147/http://www.sltrib.com/news/ci_12868837 |archive-date=2009-08-21 |access-date= |website=The Salt Lake Tribune}}</ref> where Lind researched [[pion]]-[[nucleon]] scattering in the [[Lawrence Radiation Laboratory]] and earned a PhD in [[high-energy nuclear physics]] in 1964.{{r|nasa198701}} During a leave of absence from NASA, he conducted postdoctoral research at the [[Geophysical Institute]] of the [[University of Alaska Fairbanks]] from 1975 to 1976.{{r|lindoh}}

=== Navy service ===
Upon completing his undergraduate education, Lind was initially drafted by the [[United States Army]] as a potential [[infantryman]] amid the [[Korean War]]; following "expert maneuvering," he instead enrolled at the [[United States Navy]] [[Officer Candidate School (U.S. Navy)|Officer Candidate School]] at [[Newport, Rhode Island]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Mormon on the Moon: Don Lind's Cancelled Apollo Flight | date=April 19, 2024 | url=https://hightokolob.substack.com/p/mormon-on-the-moon-apollo-20 }}</ref> After jokingly requesting flight training, Lind was unable to change his assignment and found that he enjoyed flying.<ref name="leavitt198504">{{cite news|url=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/new-era/1985/04/mission-specialist-one?lang=eng |title=Mission Specialist One |access-date=March 30, 2011 |author=Leavitt, Melvin |date=April 1985 |work=New Era |publisher=The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints |pages=28 }}</ref> He received his [[Wings of Gold]] in 1955 at [[Naval Air Station Corpus Christi]] and served four years on active duty with the Navy at [[San Diego]] and aboard the carrier [[USS Hancock (CV-19)|USS ''Hancock'']]. Lind logged more than 4,500 hours of flight time during his naval and NASA careers, 4,000 of which were in [[jet aircraft]].<ref name="nasa198701" /> He continued to serve in the [[United States Naval Reserve]] after completing his service obligation, attaining his terminal rank of [[Commander (United States)|commander]] in 1969.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Shayler |first1=David J. |title=The Last of NASA's Original Pilot Astronauts |last2=Burgess |first2=Colin |publisher=SpringerLink |year=2017 |isbn=978-3-319-51012-5 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-51014-9}}</ref>

=== NASA career ===

==== Pre-astronaut and selection ====
[[File:Skylab rescue crew.jpg|thumb|Lind with [[Vance D. Brand]] (left) as a Skylab rescue crew]]

From 1964 to 1966, Lind worked at the NASA [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] as a [[space physicist]].<ref name="utahalum"/> He was involved in experiments to determine the nature and properties of low-energy particles within the Earth's [[magnetosphere]] and [[interplanetary space]]. Lind applied for NASA's [[NASA Astronaut Group 3|third group of astronauts]] but did not have enough flight hours, and was too old for the [[NASA Astronaut Group 4|fourth group]]<ref name="lindoh"/> by 74 days, despite arguing that he would not have to learn to fly.{{r|google5}} After the age restriction changed, he was among the fifth group, the "[[NASA Astronaut Group 5|Original Nineteen]]", selected in April 1966.<ref name="moulton20090720"/><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28240973/the_high_point_enterprise/|title=19 New Spacemen Are Named|last1=Thompson|first1=Ronald|newspaper=The High Point Enterprise|location=High Point, North Carolina|date=April 5, 1966|page=2A|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>

Lind was selected as a pilot with other "Original Nineteen" astronauts{{r|google5}} in contrast to the fourth and [[NASA Astronaut Group 6|sixth]] astronaut groups, which consisted of medical doctors and Ph.D. scientists who were not qualified pilots. However, he and Group 5 colleague [[Bruce McCandless II]] (the salutatorian of his [[United States Naval Academy]] class and the recent recipient of a master's degree in [[electrical engineering]] from [[Stanford University]]) were nonetheless treated as scientist-astronauts by NASA due to their academic training and lack of [[test pilot]] experience that [[Deke Slayton]], [[Al Shepard]] and other NASA managers emphasized; among other factors, this would delay their progression in the flight rotation.<ref name="lindoh"/><ref name="google">{{cite book |author=Hersch |first=Matthew H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-dLFAAAAQBAJ |title=Inventing the American Astronaut |date=2012 |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan US |isbn=9781137025296 |access-date=January 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108191147/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=-dLFAAAAQBAJ |archive-date=January 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Apollo ====
Along with geologist-astronaut [[Harrison Schmitt]], Lind helped to develop and demonstrate the flight plan for the [[Apollo 11]] EVA (including the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Packages that would continue to relay data following the missions) and other tools used on the [[lunar surface]].<ref name="utahalum"/><ref name="google2">{{cite book |last1=Shayler |first1=David J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TweEC3h633AC&pg=PA205 |title=NASA's Scientist-Astronauts |last2=Burgess |first2=Colin |date=September 19, 2007 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=9780387493879 |page=205 |access-date=January 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108191311/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=TweEC3h633AC&pg=PA205 |archive-date=January 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> He also served as a [[capsule communicator]] on the Apollo 11 and [[Apollo 12]] missions. Schmitt, Lind and [[Owen Garriott]] were the only scientist-astronauts to receive advanced helicopter training, a key prerequisite for piloting the [[Apollo Lunar Module]].<ref name="google3">{{cite book |last1=Shayler |first1=David J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TweEC3h633AC&pg=PA244 |title=NASA's Scientist-Astronauts |last2=Burgess |first2=Colin |date=September 19, 2007 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=9780387493879 |page=244 |access-date=January 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108191924/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=TweEC3h633AC&pg=PA244 |archive-date=January 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> Due to standard crew rotations, it is believed that Lind would have followed Schmitt as the second scientist-astronaut Lunar Module Pilot on one of the [[canceled Apollo missions]] or projected long-range [[Apollo Applications Program]] lunar survey missions.{{r|google5}}<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.astronautix.com/l/lind.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161022113835/http://www.astronautix.com/l/lind.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=October 22, 2016|title=Lind|publisher=Astronautix|access-date=June 8, 2017}}</ref>

==== Skylab ====
Amid the gradual cancellation of the later Apollo missions and the devolution of the AAP into the [[Skylab program]], Lind was formally reassigned to the latter effort in August 1969; according to Slayton, who noted Lind's disappointment, "with the cancellation of [[Apollo 20|[Apollo] 20]], I could see I just wasn't going to have a flight for him".<ref name="google4">{{cite book |last1=Slayton |first1=Donald K. |author-link1=Deke Slayton |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_S-PoBi8Eu8C&pg=PA252 |title=Deke ! U.S. Manned Space From Mercury To the Shuttle |last2=Cassutt |first2=Michael |author-link2=Michael Cassutt |date=1995 |publisher=Tom Doherty Associates |isbn=9781466802148 |access-date=December 11, 2017}}</ref> Together, Lind and Group 6 scientist-astronaut [[William B. Lenoir]] comprised the Earth Resources Group of the Skylab Branch Office.<ref name=":0" />

{{quote box|align=right|width=25%|quote=[On Skylab 3 and 4,] I was backing up two of the most depressingly healthy people you can imagine.{{r|lindoh}}|author=Lind}}
Lind served as backup pilot alongside backup commander [[Vance D. Brand]] and backup science pilot Lenoir for [[Skylab 3]] and [[Skylab 4]], the second and third crewed Skylab missions; was on standby for a [[Skylab Rescue|rescue mission]] planned when malfunctions developed in Skylab 3's [[Apollo Command/Service Module]] (ultimately thwarted due to Brand and Lind's resourcefulness in devising a solution in the simulators) and the proposed 20-day [[Skylab 5]] mission (scrapped in favor of the more economical extension of Skylab 4 from 56 to 84 days); and may have flown as a pilot or science pilot on [[Skylab B]].<ref name="lindoh"/><ref name="books.google.com">{{cite book |last1=Shayler |first1=David J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TweEC3h633AC |title=NASA's Scientist-Astronauts |last2=Burgess |first2=Colin |date=2007 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=9780387493879 |access-date=January 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108191818/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=TweEC3h633AC |archive-date=January 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Astronauts knew little of why or how they were assigned to missions.{{r|kennedy19850429}}<ref name="airportjournals">{{cite web |last1=Freeze |first1= Di |title=Bill Anders: A Love of Afterburners|website=Airport Journals |date=1 April 2007 |url=http://airportjournals.com/bill-anders-a-love-of-afterburners/ |access-date=15 March 2015 }}</ref> By the Skylab era, Lind was informally perceived as a "scientist-pilot" because of his doctorate.<ref name="google6">{{cite book |author=Evans |first=Ben |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IWht0brbIfEC&pg=PA137 |title=At Home in Space: The Late Seventies into the Eighties |date=2011 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=9781441988102 |pages=137, 138, 219, 220 |access-date=January 8, 2017}}</ref> According to David Shayler, Lind "could never understand why he was not on the [Skylab 4] crew as science pilot" due to his work on the mission's Earth resources package; this could be attributed in part to seniority and specialization, as all of the prime crew science pilots were drawn from Group 4. Additionally, Skylab 4 science pilot [[Edward Gibson]] (like Lind, an atmospheric physicist) had taken on a research program in [[solar physics]] and worked on the [[Apollo Telescope Mount]] while Lind was still on track to be assigned to a lunar mission.<ref name="google5">{{cite book |author=Shayler |first=David J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X4WaYqQDVKwC&pg=PA125 |title=Skylab: America's Space Station |date=2001 |publisher=Springer |isbn=9781852334079 |pages=111, 125 |access-date=January 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170108191520/https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=X4WaYqQDVKwC&pg=PA125 |archive-date=January 8, 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> Although he cross-trained with Lenoir and briefly proposed swapping positions with his crewmate, Lind elected to retain his original assignment due to the greater likelihood of the rescue mission (which could only accommodate the commander and pilot) amid the space program's dwindling flight opportunities.<ref name="books.google.com"/>

According to [[Michael Cassutt]], in 1970, Lind "openly complained" to [[George Abbey (NASA)|George Abbey]] (then technical assistant to [[Johnson Space Center]] director [[Robert R. Gilruth]]) about the perceived administrative machinations of Slayton and Shepard and Harrison Schmitt's assignment to Apollo 17.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite book |last1=Cassutt |first1=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wtI2DwAAQBAJ&q=lind |title=Astronaut Maker: How One Mysterious Engineer Ran Human Spaceflight for a Generation |date=August 1, 2018 |publisher=Chicago Review Press |isbn=9781613737033}}</ref> However, Abbey—a close friend of Schmitt who would eventually oversee Astronaut Corps assignments as director of flight operations from 1976 to 1988—took umbrage at Lind's cooperation with a 1969 report in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' that exposed rampant dissatisfaction among the scientist-astronauts. He also alleged that Lind complained about "any and all subjects" related to the space program, associating him with a coterie of scientist-astronauts (including [[Story Musgrave]]) who perceived Abbey as a "faceless 'horse-holder' who had worked his way into a powerful job." Although Abbey could not forestall Lind's eventual flight, their acrimonious relationship played a key role in hindering the astronaut's progression in the flight rotation.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

When the [[Smithsonian Air and Space Museum]] received the unused Skylab B he "cried ceremonially in front of it", Lind later said; "I was ... in the right place at the wrong time".<ref name="upi19850430">{{cite news |date=April 30, 1985 |title=Astronaut makes it to space |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=7DlPAAAAIBAJ&pg=6946%2C5903108 |access-date=November 6, 2013 |work=The Courier |page=6B |agency=UPI}}</ref> He was reassigned to the Science and Applications Directorate in 1974, formally codifying his status as a scientist-astronaut.<ref name=":0" /> In a 1976 memo, [[Chris Kraft]] implicitly characterized Lind as one of NASA's nine active scientist-astronauts in the context of the [[payload specialist]] program.<ref name="cfu2019">{{Cite book |last1=Croft |first1=Melvin |title=Come Fly with Us: NASA's Payload Specialist Program |last2=Youskauskas |first2=John |publisher=University of Nebraska Press |year=2019 |isbn=9781496212252 |pages=22–23 |series=Outward Odyssey: a People's History of Spaceflight}}</ref>

==== Shuttle era ====
{{Main|STS-51-B}}
[[File:STS-51-B crew.jpg|thumb|right|The crew of the STS-51-B mission. Lind is at the far left]]

For the [[Space Shuttle program]], Lind was reassigned as a [[mission specialist]] along with McCandless (who, unlike Lind, continued to train as a potential [[Space Shuttle orbiter]] pilot until 1983)<ref name=":0" /> and the remaining Apollo-era scientist-astronauts. During this period, he was a member of the [[NASA Astronaut Corps|Astronaut Office]]'s Operations Missions development group, responsible for developing [[Payload (air and space craft)|payload]]s for the early Space Shuttle Orbital Flight Test (OFT) missions and the [[Canadarm]].<ref name="lindoh"/>

Lind finally flew as the lead mission specialist and de facto payload commander on [[STS-51-B]] (April 29 to May 6, 1985), logging over 168 hours in space. Due to Apollo-era managerial preferences, his contentious relationship with George Abbey, NASA budgetary problems and delays in the Space Shuttle program, Lind waited longer than any other continuously serving American astronaut for a spaceflight: 19 years.<ref name="moulton20090720"/><ref name="lindoh"/>{{refn|[[Barbara Morgan]] was selected as the backup candidate for NASA's [[Teacher in Space Project]] in July 1985 and briefly assumed [[Christa McAuliffe]]'s duties in the aftermath of the ''Challenger'' disaster before electing to return to teaching in the fall of 1986. She was then selected as a [[NASA Astronaut Group 17]] Mission Specialist in 1998 and ultimately flew on [[STS-118]] in August 2007. Although twenty-two years elapsed between her initial affiliation with NASA and her spaceflight, she was not continuously employed by the agency.}} STS-51-B's average age of 48.6 was the oldest for an American space mission.<ref name="kennedy19850429">{{Cite news |last=Kennedy |first=J. Michael |date=April 29, 1985 |title=Shuttle Flight Is Lind's First Mission : Astronaut's 19-Year Wait for Space Trip Ends Today |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1985-04-29-mn-12831-story.html |access-date=July 7, 2020 |work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref>

[[STS-51-B]], the [[Spacelab-3]] science mission, launched from [[Kennedy Space Center]], Florida, on April 29, 1985. Following several delays, this was the first fully operational [[Spacelab]] mission. The seven-man crew investigated crystal growth, drop dynamics leading to containerless material processing, atmospheric trace gas spectroscopy, solar and planetary atmospheric simulation, cosmic rays, laboratory animals and human medical monitoring.<ref name="nasa198701" />

With the help of his Alaska postdoctoral group, Lind developed and conducted an experiment to photograph the Earth's [[aurora]]. As the experiment used a camera already on the Shuttle, NASA only needed to purchase three rolls of film for $36; Lind described it as "the cheapest experiment that has ever gone into space."{{r|lindoh}} After completing 110 orbits of the Earth, the [[Space Shuttle Challenger|Orbiter ''Challenger'']] landed at [[Edwards Air Force Base]], California, on May 6, 1985.<ref name="nasa198701" />

Lind retired from NASA on the twentieth anniversary of his selection in 1986. For nine years thereafter, he served as a professor of physics and [[astronomy]] at [[Utah State University]], until his retirement in 1995.<ref name="moulton20090720"/>

== Awards and honors ==
Lind was a member of the [[American Geophysical Union]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and [[Phi Kappa Phi]]. Lind was active in the [[Boy Scouts of America]] and earned the rank of [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]].<ref>[http://www.scouting.org/About/FactSheets/scouting_space.aspx Don L. Lind at scouting.org] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303213130/http://www.scouting.org/about/factsheets/scouting_space.aspx |date=March 3, 2016 }}</ref> He was also awarded the [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]] in 1974, and the [[NASA Space Flight Medal]] following his ''Challenger'' flight.<ref name="nasa198701" />

== Personal life ==
Lind married Kathleen Maughan<ref name="moulton20090720"/> of [[Logan, Utah]], with whom he had seven children.<ref name="nasa198701" /> STS-51-B was two decades after son David's stomach aches from fear of appearing on television like the families of other astronauts, such as neighbors [[James Irwin]] and [[Edgar Mitchell]]. Kathleen said before the mission that "For our family, I think we're better off now without the publicity" as space travel became more common.{{r|kennedy19850429}}

Throughout his adult life, Lind served as a member of the lay ecclesiastical hierarchy of [[the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]]. He served as a [[Missionary (LDS Church)|missionary]] in the Northeastern United States before graduating from college (1950–52),<ref name="moulton20090720"/><ref name="lindoh">{{cite interview|url=http://www.jsc.nasa.gov/history/oral_histories/LindDL/LindDL_5-27-05.htm |title=Don L. Lind oral history transcript |publisher=NASA Johnson Space Center Oral History Project |date=May 27, 2005 |access-date=January 31, 2015 |interviewer=Wright, Rebecca |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150201141641/http://www.jsc.nasa.gov/history/oral_histories/LindDL/LindDL_5-27-05.htm |archive-date=February 1, 2015 }}</ref> and after STS-51-B spoke in [[General Conference (LDS Church)|General Conference]] about his experience.<ref name="lind198510">{{cite web|url=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/general-conference/1985/10/the-heavens-declare-the-glory-of-god?lang=eng |title=The Heavens Declare the Glory of God |access-date=March 30, 2011 |author=Lind, Don |date=October 1985 |work=October 1985 General Conference |publisher=The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints }}</ref> He and his wife Kathleen served as public affairs missionaries in the Europe West Area of the Church, as temple missionaries in the [[Nauvoo Illinois Temple]], and, respectively, as a counselor and an assistant matron in the presidency of the [[Portland Oregon Temple]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fairmormon.org/testimonies/scholars/don-l-lind |title=Mormon Scholars Testify / Don L. Lind |access-date=April 19, 2020 |date= January 2010|publisher=FairMormon }}</ref> During his Astronaut Corps service, Lind frequently spoke at LDS Church events throughout the United States.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Mar 07, 1975, page 6 - The Idaho Statesman at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com | url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/912825690/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250618221626/https://www.newspapers.com/image/912825690/ | access-date=2025-09-07 | archive-date=2025-06-18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Aug 01, 1981, page 3 - Petaluma Argus-Courier at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com | url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/247032695/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250618221626/https://www.newspapers.com/image/247032695/ | access-date=2025-09-07 | archive-date=2025-06-18}}</ref>
Lind's wife Kathleen died on June 12, 2022.<ref>{{cite news |title=Don Lind, shuttle astronaut whose moon mission was canceled, dies at 92 |url=http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-090222a-astronaut-don-lind-obituary.html |access-date=September 4, 2022 |work=collectSPACE.com |date=September 2, 2022}}</ref>

Lind died on August 30, 2022, in [[Logan, Utah]], with many of his children and grandchildren at his bedside.  His funeral was planned for September 10 in [[Smithfield, Utah|Smithfield]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Logan |last=Stefanich |date=September 3, 2022 |newspaper=Deseret News |title=Decorated Utah astronaut Don Lind dies at 92 |url=https://www.deseret.com/utah/2022/9/2/23334977/utah-astronaut-don-lind-dies |access-date=September 4, 2022}}</ref>
